title: Ego leaves in good company
hook: in the holy company ego departs and wisdom comes

segments.voice: Yesterday, saadh sangat: in the holy company the face grows bright and the grime washes off. Your line was company shapes you. Today, the same stanza goes deeper, past the face.

Two dinner tables. At the first, one guest talks the whole time: their job, their trip, their opinions. Everyone else nods. At the second, the oldest person there mostly listens, asks good questions, and laughs at other people's stories. Something odd happens at that second table. Nobody tries to win. The loud ones get quieter without being told. By dessert, people are saying things they've never said out loud. Nobody fought anybody's ego. It just left the room. Ashtpadi seven's first stanza has a line about where pride goes in good company.
screen: `ONE GUEST TALKS ALL NIGHT.` → `ANOTHER TABLE, ONE WHO LISTENS.` → `NOBODY FOUGHT THE EGO.`

segments.voice: After the bright face and the washed grime, the stanza continues. Saadh kai sang mitai abhimaan: in the company of the holy, pride is erased. Abhimaan is pride, self-importance, the need to be the one who matters most. Mitai means it's rubbed out, the way chalk disappears from a board. Next: saadh kai sang pragtai sugiaan. In the holy company, true wisdom shows itself. Sugiaan is good knowing, real understanding. Pragtai means it comes into view, as if it had been there all along, just hidden. And then: in the holy company, God is understood to be near. So the order runs: first pride goes, then wisdom appears, then God feels close. Sikh teaching speaks of haumai, the ego that walls the self off, and here is one way the wall comes down: not by attacking it, but by sitting where it has nothing to do. In good company there's no one to compete with, so pride gets bored and wanders off. That's why the carry says quietly. You won't usually notice the moment. You'll just realize, on the way home, that you didn't need to be right tonight, and that you heard something wise you'd have missed if you were talking. One way to live this stanza is to take the listening seat.
screen: `ABHIMAAN: PRIDE, RUBBED OUT.` · `SUGIAAN: WISDOM COMES INTO VIEW.` · `THEN GOD IS FELT NEAR.` · `NOTHING FOR PRIDE TO DO.` · then, large: `EGO LEAVES QUIETLY.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and listen: the nearest sound, the farthest, the sound under all the others, without naming or judging them, and notice how little of you is needed to listen. That's the listening seat, and it fits any conversation: let the other person finish, wait a breath, ask a question instead of telling a story. If you pray, you can listen for the Name in the quiet.
Abhimaan, pride, self-importance. In the holy company it's rubbed out, and wisdom, sugiaan, comes into view.
Your line: ego leaves quietly. Pride has nothing to do at a table where no one is trying to win. Day four hundred sixty-four, in the book.

howItsDone: In the sangat, Sikhs sit together on the floor, without ranked seating, to listen to kirtan and katha; many describe that shared listening as where pride softens.

chat.says: How do you get rid of a big ego? Do you just keep fighting it until it gives up?
options: The stanza says it leaves in good company: with no one to compete with, pride has nothing to do.
Win more arguments; once people see you're right, you won't need to prove it anymore.
Avoid people entirely, since company is what feeds the ego in the first place.
